logline: A Japanese figure skater who collapsed at the Grand Prix Finals returns home in defeat, only to have his idol - five-time world champion Victor Nikiforov - show up at his family's inn and offer to coach him back to the podium.

renewal.note: The 12-episode series concluded in December 2016. The sequel film 'Ice Adolescence' was announced in 2017 and officially cancelled by MAPPA in April 2024 due to creative reasons. No Season 2 has been announced.

bollymeter.basis: Yuri on Ice holds an IMDb rating of 8.2 and a MAL score of 7.90 from nearly a million users; five of nine Anime News Network reviewers named it the season's best show, and professional figure skaters including Johnny Weir praised it for competitive authenticity.

seasons.review_body: Yuri on Ice premiered on TV Asahi in October 2016, as an original MAPPA series directed by Sayo Yamamoto and written by Mitsuro Kubo. The series is frequently singled out among standout anime of its decade, with Crunchyroll including it on its top-25 anime of the 2010s list. Its on-ice tension and performance anxiety are rendered with an authentic feeling, and it also earned recognition for the care it takes with its emotional beats. The story attracted major attention for portraying an explicit same-sex romantic relationship, highlighted by a public kiss and an exchange of rings that stand out for mainstream anime. It also resists easy labeling as yaoi while keeping the Victor and Yuuri relationship at the center without ambiguity. The series won awards at the Tokyo Anime Award Festival and the Crunchyroll Anime Awards.

episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere opens on defeat rather than triumph - Yuuri finishing last at the Grand Prix Final - and spends its first half in the quiet humiliation of returning home. The arrival of Victor at the inn is staged as absurdist comedy before pivoting into something warmer. The skate sequences use animation to capture the kinetic specificity of competitive figure skating.
episode_reviews.the_moment: Victor appearing at the onsen - the series establishing its romantic premise through physical comedy rather than confession.
episode_reviews.review_body:
# Yuri On Ice S1E1: "Easy as Pirozhki!! The Grand Prix Final of Tears" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

Katsuki Yuri has reached the Grand Prix Final for the first time, and the premiere places that achievement beside humiliation. A newscaster marks the milestone. Yuri answers with his own name after being labeled last. That cut tells us how the episode will treat him: accomplishment and collapse arrive in the same breath. **Katsuki Yuri** is introduced as a skater with enough talent to reach the top level and enough damage to wonder whether getting there was worth it.

BollyAI's read: the episode works because it treats failure as a living condition, then lets the final minute weaponizes hope.

## Last Place Is the Opening Move

The premiere begins with a cruel little equation. Yuri earns a Grand Prix Final spot for the first time, then becomes the skater introduced through last place. The writing does not need a speech to make that sting. The milestone is real. The embarrassment is real. Their collision is the character.

Yuri's self-description sharpens the wound: "I'm one of the dime-a-dozen top figure skaters." The line is funny in the most miserable way. It carries pride and self-disgust in one breath. He knows he belongs somewhere near greatness, but he talks like someone lowering the room's expectations before the room can hurt him again.

The episode's best early choice is to make pressure physical. Yuri connects failure to binge eating, to his body, to the kind of collapse that follows him off the ice. That grounds the drama. Defeat here has residue. It affects how he moves, how he talks, and how he tries to disappear.

The title promises tears, and the first act earns them without turning Yuri into a saint of suffering. He is prickly, embarrassed, and already tired of being read by other people. That messiness gives the premiere its bite.

## The Quitter Who Keeps Skating

The core tension is clean: Yuri keeps moving while refusing to decide where he is going. After being told to retire, he hears the counter-push: "It's too early for you to retire!" The line matters because the episode does not let it solve him. Encouragement lands. The pressure that broke him remains.

That restraint is the premiere's sharpest craft instinct. Yuri argues that retirement is premature, yet he turns away from immediate decisions. He wants to keep going while managing real uncertainty about whether skating will continue for him. That tension is richer than a clean comeback vow. He does not stand up, point at the rink, and announce destiny. He hesitates.

The show proves persistence through behavior rather than speeches. Yuri returns home. He says he needs time. He considers skating only part-time. He also keeps practicing and stays focused on skating after coming back. The writing understands that denial and devotion can share the same pair of skates. Yuri can be exhausted by the sport and still unable to leave it alone.

The episode does strain under its setup. The early stretch carries heavy exposition about failures, qualifications, and emotional state, with quiet gaps and abrupt confrontations. The rhythm sometimes feels like the episode is unpacking a suitcase in the hallway. Necessary items arrive, but not always gracefully.

## Hasetsu Makes Defeat Smaller Without Making It Easy

After five years, **Minako-sensei** welcomes Yuri back and asks why he is skulking around. That detail does a lot of work. Home is no victory lap. It is a place where people know him well enough to cut through his performance. Yuri can hide from the Grand Prix Final result, but he cannot quite hide from a teacher who sees the shape of his avoidance.

The homecoming changes the scale of the episode. The Grand Prix Final is public, formal, and humiliating. Hasetsu is personal. Moving back home makes Yuri's crisis less spectacular and more uncomfortable. He has to answer ordinary questions. He has to exist in spaces that remember him from before the collapse.

The Vicchan beat fits that smaller register. Being told to go say hi to Vicchan, then promising to think things over about skating, gives the episode a softer way to hold indecision. Yuri is choosing among retirement, competition, and the life waiting around him. That life contains obligations, affection, memory, and delay.

That is why the slower middle works better emotionally than structurally. On a plotting level, the episode can feel stop-start as it moves between failure recap, homecoming conversation, and practice. On a character level, the pauses make sense. Yuri is skulking because he has not found a heroic posture yet. Good. The episode is stronger for denying him one.

## Alone on the Ice, Still in the Story

The rink material gives the premiere its clearest image of Yuri's inner state. The line "You just want to skate alone for now right?" identifies his instinct without overexplaining it. He wants the sport without the demand. Movement without judgment. He wants to recover the love of skating before deciding whether the competitive machine gets another chance to chew him up.

That distinction matters. Yuri does not stop skating after his season ends badly. He keeps practicing as a way of coping with failure. Skating becomes less a career decision than a private argument with himself. Every return to the ice says what he cannot say out loud: he is not done, even when he cannot promise he will continue.

The episode also plants the season's key question here. If Yuri keeps skating, how will he handle pressure the next time it comes for him? The premiere has already shown that talent and opportunity do not protect him from collapse. A Grand Prix Final berth did not make him secure. It made the fall more visible.

BollyAI's read: this is where the episode earns its final twist. Victor's arrival would feel cheap if Yuri had done nothing but mope. Instead, the premiere spends time showing him in motion. The coach arrives after the skater has already, quietly, refused to disappear.

## Victor Enters Like a Full Stop That Becomes a Starting Gun

The last minute is shameless in the right way. **Victor Nikiforov** appears in Hasetsu and says, "Yuri starting today I'm your coach." It is direct, absurdly confident, and the interruption this episode has been winding toward. Yuri has spent the episode asking for time. Victor arrives and turns uncertainty into structure.

The episode frames Victor as a genius who never failed to surprise Yuri, which makes the ending feel explosive rather than random. This is Yuri's ideal stepping into his stalled life and declaring a plan. The final promise is pressure with a face.

That matters because Victor's stated aim is not modest. He wants to coach Yuri and make him win the Grand Prix Final. After an episode built on last place, failed qualifications, and a season that ended with "Going Home!", the goal has the clean force of provocation. It does not erase Yuri's fears. It challenges them.

The "To Be Continued!!!" button fits the premiere's personality: theatrical, cheeky, aware that it has kicked open the door. If the middle occasionally strains under its own setup, the ending lands because that setup has been emotionally specific. Victor arrives at the exact point where persistence needs direction.

## The Verdict

"Easy as Pirozhki!! The Grand Prix Final of Tears" is a strong premiere because it refuses the simplest comeback shape. Yuri does not lose, cry, train, and reset in a straight line. He loses, returns home, avoids decisions, keeps skating, and only then gets hit by Victor's impossible certainty. That order is the craft.

The episode's weakness is pacing. Its exposition-heavy stretches and abrupt tonal turns make parts of the middle feel overpacked, especially around the failure recap and confrontational beats. Still, the character spine holds. The final scene works because Yuri's uncertainty has been treated seriously.

BollyAI's score: 8.1. As a season opener, it plants the essential arc cleanly: Yuri must decide whether skating can become love again before it becomes competition again.

Written by BollyAI, reviewed by our editorial team.

verdict.one_liner: A sharp premiere turns Yuri's humiliation into motion, then lets Victor arrive as pressure with a plan.

episode_reviews.title: China's on Fire!! Grand Prix Series, Cup of China Free Skate
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The episode that catalysed the series' cultural moment - Yuuri's free skate performance of 'Yuri on Ice,' the post-performance embrace with Victor, and the ambiguous moment that became the most-discussed image from any anime in 2016. Critics and audiences processed it as a kiss or near-kiss; the series never clarified and never needed to.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The post-skate embrace - the moment that made Yuri on Ice a landmark for LGBTQ representation in mainstream anime.

episode_reviews.title: Gotta Super-Supercharge It!! Grand Prix Final Free Skate
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale delivers Yuuri's final competitive skate and the clearest statement of the Victor-Yuuri relationship the series allows. The resolution is deliberately imperfect in competitive terms while being emotionally complete, landing as earned and satisfying.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The ring exchange - the series committing to its romantic premise with a gesture that had no equivalent in prior anime.
